lessons.title: What is a block
lessons.summary: A block is a header plus a list of transactions, and its room - 4,000,000 weight units - is the blockspace everyone competes for.
objectives: Name the parts of a block - the 80-byte header, the coinbase transaction and the other transactions.
State the consensus limit on a block's size - 4,000,000 weight units.
Explain why a miner fills a block with the transactions that pay the highest fee rate.

lessons.title: Weight units and the 4,000,000 WU limit
lessons.summary: Bitcoin measures transactions in weight units - 4 per non-witness byte, 1 per witness byte - and wallets quote virtual bytes, weight divided by four.
objectives: Compute a transaction's weight from its non-witness and witness bytes.
Convert weight to virtual bytes (vbytes), rounding up.
Explain why a block with no witness data holds at most 1,000,000 bytes.

lessons.title: Why witness bytes weigh less
lessons.summary: SegWit made signature data four times cheaper than the data that creates outputs - which is why modern transactions are smaller and inscriptions live in the witness.
objectives: Explain why witness data is discounted relative to non-witness data.
Compare the virtual size of the same payment made with P2PKH, P2WPKH and P2TR.
Explain why inscription content is placed in the witness.

lessons.title: Fees, vbytes and the fee market
lessons.summary: A fee is whatever the inputs hold beyond the outputs; miners rank it per virtual byte, so fee = fee rate x vsize, rounded up.
objectives: Compute a fee from a fee rate and a virtual size, rounding up.
Explain why the fee is implicit - inputs minus outputs.
Describe how replace-by-fee and child-pays-for-parent speed up a stuck transaction.

lessons.title: UTXOs and sats
lessons.summary: Bitcoin has no accounts - a wallet holds unspent outputs, each spent whole, measured in sats, with change coming back as a new output.
objectives: Explain what a UTXO is and how an outpoint identifies it.
Work out the change output of a payment, including when change is too small to keep.
State the P2TR dust limit and why it exists.

lessons.title: Ordinal theory and sat order (FIFO)
lessons.summary: Ordinal theory numbers every sat in the order it was mined and tracks it through transactions first in, first out.
objectives: State the first-in-first-out rule for how input sats flow into outputs.
Predict which output, and at which offset, an inscribed sat lands in.
Explain why putting a funding input first can burn an inscription to the fee.

lessons.title: Inscriptions and the envelope
lessons.summary: An inscription is content carried in an inert OP_FALSE OP_IF envelope inside a tapscript, split into pushes of at most 520 bytes.
objectives: Read the parts of an envelope - the ord marker, the tags and the body.
Explain why content is split into chunks of at most 520 bytes.
Explain why an envelope must live in a tapscript.

lessons.title: Commit and reveal
lessons.summary: Inscribing takes two transactions - a commit that pays to a taproot output hiding the envelope, and a reveal that spends it and publishes the content.
objectives: Explain why an inscription needs a commit transaction and a reveal transaction.
Name the three witness items of a script-path spend.
Compute a reveal's weight, lane and fee from its envelope length.

lessons.title: Parents, children and provenance
lessons.summary: A child inscription names its parent in tag 3 and its reveal spends the parent - on-chain proof that the collection's holder made it.
objectives: Encode a parent inscription id into the bytes of the parent tag.
Explain why spending the parent in the reveal proves authorship.
Explain why the parent-return output must carry exactly the parent's value.

lessons.title: PSBTs: what your wallet signs
lessons.summary: A PSBT lets a service build a transaction and your wallet sign it; the sighash flag on each signature decides what can still be changed.
objectives: Describe what a PSBT carries and why it lets a service stay non-custodial.
Read a sighash flag and say which inputs and outputs a signature covers.
List what to check before signing a PSBT.

lessons.title: Custody: keys, seeds and what never to share
lessons.summary: Your recovery words and private keys are the wallet; addresses are safe to share, extended public keys are private, and no honest service ever asks for the words.
objectives: Sort wallet data into safe to share, private, and never to share.
Compute how much entropy a 12- or 24-word recovery phrase carries.
Recognise requests for recovery words as a scam, whoever makes them.

lessons.title: Measuring blockspace (the Meter and certification)
lessons.summary: block.space's Meter attributes the chain's bytes to protocols in books and denominations, and its certification signs reproducible statistics about collections.
objectives: Explain why bytes and vbytes are reported separately and cannot be converted without the witness split.
Compute a collection's statistics the way a certification attestation defines them.
Describe how anyone can verify and reproduce a certification.
